outcomes.rationale: Integrity: both render fully, but each has one blemish. A's slide 10 breaks its numbered list — item 1 is numbered ('1. Approve the three-year glide path…', with the trailing 'per slide 8.' orphaned on its own line) while the following three asks lose their numbers and sit at a different indent, so the closing ask page reads as a malformed list. B has no comparable rendering fault. Legibility: comparable and both marginal in places — A's slide 4 grouped-bar data labels and slide 7 body copy are small, B's slide 7 constraint-box text and slide 3 axis labels are equally small; nothing fails outright. Coherence: B is the more disciplined chrome — every page carries the same kicker, blue title, and '01 / 10 · CAPITAL ALLOCATION REVIEW · SEPTEMBER 2026' footer, and the green title-bar/second-series accent is used consistently. A is also consistent (kicker, blue rule under the title slide, footers) but loses points for the slide 10 list. Communicative effectiveness is where A pulls ahead: its exec summary (slide 2) leads each paragraph with a bolded claim, slide 3 pairs the bar chart with a per-division read-out ('19% Division A — highest return, 22% of capital'), slides 5 and 6 give the same EUR 120m twice with total rows and a blended-return callout (11.8% → 14.3%), slide 8 tables the three-year glide path with a Year 3 target column, and slide 9 attaches '+2.5 pts' and 'EUR 0 additional capital required' to the line chart. B by contrast leaves slide 2 with three thin bullets over an empty lower half, slide 10 with three bullets over the same void, and spends slide 3 on a chart whose bars are near-identical by design, then admits in a note that the return data — the actual subject of the deck — is 'not shown'. Distinctiveness: A's stat pills on the title page, right-hand annotation boxes, implication bar on slide 7 and closing statement bar on slide 10 make it read as built for this brief; B's mono footers give it a house style but slides 2, 7 and 10 read as a template with the blanks filled. A wins, but only slightly: the broken numbering on its recommendation slide is exactly the kind of defect a client notices, and it nearly cancels its content advantage.

Both clear integrity and legibility: no clipping, no placeholders, consistent eyebrow/title/footer/page-number systems, and readable type at projection size (A's slide 8 table and slide 6 footnote and B's slide 8 axis labels are the smallest type in either, but both hold). Coherence is close — A is marginally tighter (the blue metric strip repeats identically on slides 5/6/7, the three option cards on slide 4 share one card spec), while B's slide 9 leaves the middle and right columns nearly empty against a full left column, the one place its rhythm slips. The decision comes at level 4. The brief asks for the competitor's position and P&L impact over two years, and B actually shows it: slide 3 plots the six-point share transfer as two labelled series over four quarters, slide 5 charts the discount-vs-burn economics with the 22% floor called out, slide 8 charts Year-1 vs Year-2 P&L per option with signed dollar values, and slide 7's table carries absolute figures ($299M ARR, $58M at risk, -$28M net two-year P&L) with units. A carries only one chart in ten slides (slide 3), and its option slides quantify in relative terms only ("Year 1 revenue -1%", "-4.5 pts") — the two-year comparison is confined to the small slide 8 table, so the central economic argument is asserted in prose rather than shown. B's titles also conclude more often ("Below a 22% discount, every Halyard win loses them money", "Option A protects the most value at the lowest margin cost") where A's option slides label rather than conclude ("Option 1 of 3 — Speed"). On distinctiveness, A's slides 5/6/7 are the same two-column "What this buys us / What it costs us" frame three times and would survive any brief; B names the entrant, the segment, the owners and the September 30 deadline (slide 10's ask table with named officers and dates), so it reads as made for this decision. B is clearly the one to send; A is clean but thinner as an argument and more generic.

Neither deck fails integrity: nothing in B or A is clipped, empty or placeholdered, and both carry declarative titles. They separate at levels 2-5.

Legibility is the one place A leads. B's slide 2 EBITDA chart is the weakest artefact in either deck — a narrow plot with roughly eight crowded y-axis ticks and a hairline two-series legend that will not read from the back of a room of twenty; B's slide 5 governance boxes (five owner cards each holding name, role, workstream and amount) and the slide 6 cadence table also run small and light-grey. A's slide 3 chart is larger, has three axis labels instead of eight, and carries the '-6 pts' callout inside the plot. This is a real but bounded deficit for B, not a failure.

B then wins level 3 outright. Its eyebrow kickers ('WHY NOW', 'THE TARGET', 'GOVERNANCE', 'ACCOUNTABILITY') sit in the same position on every page, the black cover and black closer bookend a consistent monochrome system, and the tables on 6, 8, 9 and 10 share one rule weight and column rhythm. A is coherent within pages but its colour is unsystematic: slide 5's bar chart assigns five arbitrary hues (blue, orange, green, yellow, red) to workstreams that carry no colour meaning anywhere else, while slide 7's org chart re-uses blue/orange/green for a different cut, and slide 8's forum table has heavy default gridlines that appear nowhere else in the deck.

At level 4 both have a flaw. B stretches accountability across slides 8 and 9 with only two rows each and a large unexplained vertical gap between them — a page and a half of near-empty table where one dense slide would do. A duplicates its own content: slide 5 (bar chart of the split) and slide 6 (table of the same split) say the same thing twice, and slide 2 is a filler agenda. A's slide 6 total row (EUR 40M / 100%) is a genuine advantage — it closes the arithmetic, which B's slide 4 table never does. Roughly even, with B slightly ahead on titles that state a conclusion ('Procurement carries the largest share; four other workstreams complete the EUR 40m', 'Each owner carries two hard dates, not a general direction') and on naming actual owners (Elena Marsh, CPO; Raj Kapoor, COO) rather than A's generic 'Head of Procurement', 'CHRO'.

Level 5 decides it. B reads as composed for this brief: the €40m and -6.0 pts set as editorial display figures, the dark cover/closer, the three-card 90-day board. A reads as a corporate template with the blanks filled — blue title cover, agenda slide, footer page numbers, SmartArt-style org chart, bordered default table. On genericness A is markedly the more interchangeable of the two; swap the numbers and it would serve any programme kickoff. I would send B with edits (enlarge the slide 2 chart, merge slides 8 and 9); I would not send A unchanged with my name on it.

Both clear level 1: nothing clipped, overlapping or left as placeholder in either deck, and both are readable, though the axis tick text in B's slide 4 (weeks to first value) and slide 8 (% of lost-deal reasons) is smaller than A's larger chart plots — A's only legibility edge. The separation comes at level 3 and 4. A is structurally uneven: slides 5, 7, 9 and 11 are four short bullets parked in the top third with the entire lower half of the page empty, and the three cards on slide 3 carry a headline at the top of each box with a large dead grey area beneath, so the repeated element reads as unfilled. A's slide 1 is centred with an italic subtitle while every other page is left-aligned — a one-off. B holds one system across all eleven pages: italic kicker, left-aligned conclusion title, evidence block, footer, and it fills the frame (slide 3 and 11 use numbered 01/02/03 lines, slide 6 pairs a ranked reason list with a pull quote). On communicative effectiveness B is ahead: its chart on slide 8 carries an explicit source line ('win-loss coding on closed-lost deals'), slides 4 and 6 attach verbatim interview quotes as evidence with an attribution line, and the slide 10 table adds a Priority column that turns findings into a roadmap call, where A's table stops at 'Roadmap priority' prose. A does have punchier stat treatments (+125% on slide 4, #1 on slide 6, 40% vs 11% on slide 8) and numbered footers with a date, which B lacks — but that is a level-5 flourish over a level-3 weakness. Neither is distinctive: both are monochrome grey-box decks that would suit any research readout, with B marginally less so because of the quote and source apparatus.

Both decks are clean at the integrity level — no clipping, no placeholder text, no overlap visible in either — so the decision is made at levels 3–5. Level 2: A's small print (the eyebrow labels, chart axis labels on p4/p5/p9/p10, footers) is very light grey and set small, and A's table body on p13/p14 is tight; B's type is marginally more comfortable but B has its own legibility hit, notably the reversed phase blocks on p10 where 'Phase 1 / Discovery & Design / Months 1–6' is white 6pt-scale text on dark grey inside a small band, and the p6 alternatives table crams 5-year cost, verdict and rationale into very tight rows. Neither fails outright; call it a wash. Level 3: A is more coherent — a consistent eyebrow-label + statement-title system on every page (EXECUTIVE SUMMARY, THE COST OF STANDING STILL, ALTERNATIVES CONSIDERED…), a repeating stat-tile pattern that appears on p2, p3 and returns deliberately on the closing p15, and a consistent rule under the title. B has no eyebrow system, so p1's 'INVESTMENT COMMITTEE · CORE PLATFORM MODERNIZATION' kicker is orphaned, and B's page-to-page structure oscillates: p2, p3, p11, p13 are plain bullet stacks with no visual device, while p8 and p9 are chart pages — the deck reads as alternating 'bullets' and 'chart' rather than a designed system. B's p2 also stacks four bullets and then three stat tiles with a large empty band between them. Level 4: A is stronger where it matters for an investment committee. A's titles are conclusions ('Doing nothing still costs EUR 25m over six years — and that is the conservative number', 'Waiting doesn't reduce the risk. It concentrates it.', 'Replace is the only option that meets every criterion'); B's are more often labels ('A 14-Year-Old Platform Now Runs the Whole Business', 'One Steering Committee, Three Workstreams'). A also annotates: every chart on p5, p9, p10 carries an italic footnote stating assumptions and units ('Assumes a flat EUR 4.2m a year…', 'Net of the EUR 23m investment…'), and p12 gates carry explicit approval criteria and the caveat 'No tranche releases automatically'. B's charts are less consistently sourced — p8's phased-cost bar chart has an axis with no unit label beyond the caption, and p9's crossover chart legend ('Replace / Do nothing') is tiny relative to the point being made. A's risk treatment is also better structured: p13 gives likelihood/impact/why-it-matters and p14 gives a matching owner/mitigation table on the same rows, an explicit pairing B compresses into one p12 table. B does add a useful p14 tracking-metrics table A lacks. Level 5: both are restrained monochrome, but A's dark p1 cover with the thin rule, the recurring three-tile motif closing on 'Today — Decision requested', and the checkmark list on p8 give it a small amount of intent; B's p1 is a plain left-aligned white title page and the deck reads closer to a default template with the blanks filled. Generic-ness: both are template-shaped, but B is the more generic of the two — strip the words and B's bullet-and-footer pages could serve any topic, whereas A's cost-of-inaction curve, gate table and paired risk spreads are shaped to this brief. I would send neither entirely unchanged, but A is the closer of the two.

Both decks are structurally sound at Level 1–2: neither shows clipped text, empty frames or placeholder strings, and both hold reading order. B's black chapter dividers (slides 3, 7, 11) are high-contrast and legible; A's dark navy title (slide 1) likewise. So the decision is made at Levels 3–5.

Level 3 (coherence) slightly favours B: its eyebrow-kicker + rule + title system repeats identically on every slide, and the 41%/34%/25% share-bar strip on slides 8/9/10 is a genuinely disciplined repeated element. But B has coherence defects too — the stat-plus-body slides (5, 8, 9, 10) leave large empty right-hand and lower zones with a lone paragraph floating in them, and slide 5's '€92M / +42% / ~12%' boxes sit awkwardly against the left stat with different weights, so the module reads hand-placed. A's system (kicker, title, footer, consistent card/table treatments, lever colour coding) also repeats reliably, and its colour discipline is stronger: each lever is bound to a colour (Expansion green, Adjacent orange, Pricing blue) and that binding is carried through the bridge chart (slide 5), the summary table (slide 2), the quadrant (slide 10), the stacked phasing chart (slide 11), the risk table (slide 12) and the approval cards (slide 13). That is a real cross-page grammar rather than repetition of a frame.

Level 4 is where the gap becomes decisive. Both write conclusion-style titles, but A's carry more argument: 'Reaching €310m means growing at ~12% — not 4%' (4), 'Expansion is the best risk-adjusted bet' (10), 'Expansion leads early; segments scale through year three' (11), 'Two of the three levers need the board's approval to move' (13). B's titles are more descriptive — 'Existing-customer expansion: 41% of the plan', 'Two adjacent segments: 34% of the plan' — three near-identical slides that restate a share the executive summary already gave. On evidence: A supplies four distinct chart/table types (waterfall bridge, confidence-vs-investment quadrant, stacked three-year phasing, checkpoint table) plus a full lever comparison matrix on slide 2; B supplies exactly one chart, the bridge on slide 6, and it is rendered in flat greys where the encoding ('Darker accent = higher confidence') has to be explained in a caption because the palette does nothing on its own. B's slide 12 trade-off table is good, but B's slides 8/9/10 spend three full pages on what A compresses into slide 6 plus slide 2, freeing A to add phasing, risk mitigation and a tracking cadence. The brief asked for an executive summary the board could read alone: A's slide 2 has the full table (share, contribution, confidence, investment) plus a bolded ASK line; B's slide 2 has three number boxes and three bullets, thinner on the investment/confidence dimension the brief specifically called for. A also closes the loop the brief implies — slide 13 names which levers need approval and which do not, slide 14 sets checkpoints with proof points; B's asks on slide 14 are looser ('Agree a quarterly review cadence').

Level 5: B is the more striking artefact — the giant ghosted 01/02/03 numerals and the black dividers give it a designed, editorial feel that A's conventional consulting layout lacks. But that comes at a cost: B burns three of fifteen slides on dividers that carry no content, and the monochrome-plus-grey palette makes the one chart weaker. A is less visually daring and its stat-plus-bullets slides (7, 8, 9) are close to stock, but nothing on A reads as unfinished.

Net: B wins on visual flair, A wins on the levels that outrank flair — argument-bearing titles, chart variety that actually earns its space, a consistent semantic colour system, and a closing sequence that tells the board what to approve and how it will be tracked. I would send A with my name on it after tightening slide 9's near-empty lower half; B I would send back for its three redundant source slides and its single grey chart.

On genericness: both are recognisably 'board deck', but B is the more generic of the two in substance despite looking less generic on the surface — swap the numbers and B's five near-identical stat slides work for any strategy brief unchanged. A's lever-colour system, quadrant and phasing chart are built around this specific three-source argument and would not transfer without rework.

Integrity: both render cleanly with no clipping, empty frames or placeholder text. B's page 5 chart (Ambition vs Reality) and page 7 scatter render, as do A's page 4 bar chart and page 6 bubble map, so neither fails level 1. Legibility separates them: B sets nearly all body copy very small — page 2's executive summary paragraphs, page 8's two-column project table (10 rows of tiny figures split across two columns), page 10's under-2-years table and page 12's numbered steps all sit at a size that would be unreadable projected; the footers and eyebrows are near-vanishing. A holds a larger, consistent body size, uses numbered chips and short bullet lines, and its tables (page 10 reallocation, page 12 ask) stay readable. Coherence: A repeats a clear system — blue title/close bookends, coloured eyebrow rule, a full-width blue action bar on pages 2, 5, 7, 8, 9, 11 — and repeats it faithfully; B is coherent too but flatter, with more variance in how each decision page is built (page 8 is a dense two-column table, page 9 a wide table, page 10 another split table, so the three parallel decisions look unlike each other). Communicative effectiveness: A's decision pages 7/8/9 lead with the huge numeral (11 / 4 / 8), a one-line qualifier with % of portfolio, evidence bullets and a named Action bar — the parallelism makes the stop/fund/hold argument legible in one pass; B's equivalents dump project-level rows without a stated action. B does have real strengths A lacks: page 4 cites a source line ('Source: FY2026 portfolio ledger') and B's page 11 reallocation table shows explicit before/after/change columns, while A's page 10 table carries a caveat that today's figures are illustrative. A also risks a units slip — page 3's '€2M REVENUE' stat and page 6's axis labels are thin on units versus B's more careful '€6.1m/yr' notation. But those are level-4 details against B's level-2 legibility problem, and the rubric ranks the lower level first. Craft: A's cover (blue field, three stat columns), the coloured vertical rule on the decision pages and the closing 'The ask' page read as composed for this brief; B's near-monochrome black-on-white with red/green accents is restrained and competent but its slide 1 black block and generic footers read closer to a stock frame. Neither is fully distinctive — both are recognisably consulting-deck furniture — but A is the one I would send with fewer edits.

Integrity: both render without clipping, but A's slide 7 has visible strain — the three criteria cards ('Market attractiveness — 25%', 'Competitive favourability — 35%', 'Capability fit — 40%') have body text crammed to the card edges, and the donut chart legend sits at a size that is barely resolvable next to it. A's slide 10 packs a three-card row plus a three-column sub-caption row plus a three-bullet block into one slide, giving four competing text sizes. B has no comparable overfill.

Legibility: A is systematically smaller. Chart axis labels on A slides 4/5/6, the source lines, and the slide 8 table body all sit at a size that will not survive projection; A slide 8's table is a full 4-column x 3-row scoring matrix in small type with a two-line methodology footnote beneath. B's charts (5, 6, 8) use large data labels sitting directly above the bars and drop the y-axis entirely, which reads at distance. B's slide 4 comparison table has generous row height and readable body text.

Coherence: both are consistent, but A mixes chart treatments — slides 4, 5, 6 and 9 all use gridded axes with rotated axis titles, while slide 7 introduces a donut and slide 10 introduces coloured pill cards, so the deck changes visual language three times. B holds one system throughout: green eyebrow, black title, left-rule cards (slides 7 and 10), same bar treatment on 5/6/8, same 'ADJACENT MARKET SCAN nn / 10' footer on every page.

Communicative effectiveness is where the gap opens. A's titles are largely descriptive of the chart ('Segment B's pool is 3.4x Segment A and 6.5x Segment C', 'Segment C grows more than 2x faster') — they state the datum, not the consequence — and slide 9's title ('C and A are within 0.05 points of each other') buries the lede. B's titles conclude: 'Segment C leads on both growth and capability fit; Segment B trails on both', 'Segment C scores highest — capability fit and growth outweigh raw scale', 'Prioritize Segment C for entry in the next planning cycle'. B's slide 2 executive summary gives three colour-coded verdict cards (DEPRIORITIZE / HOLD — SCALE OPTION / PRIORITIZE — ENTER FIRST) with the numbers on them, so the answer is on slide 2. B's slide 3 states the four weights and what each measures, and B's slide 8 footnote gives the exact weighting (overlap 30%, growth 25%, entry ease 20%, size 25%) plus 'Bars show % of the maximum score' — the unit is declared. A's slide 8 shows a weighted score of 3.35 vs 3.45 without ever stating the scale is 1-5 in the title, and the margin is 0.10 on a 5-point scale, which A then calls a tie.

B is also the more defensible recommendation: it commits to C and explains the scale/fit trade-off, with a 90-day go/no-go path on slide 10 that has owners-by-phase. A's slide 2 recommendation ('Enter Segment A first; track Segment C as a fast-follow') contradicts its own slide 6 finding that capability transfers best into C, and slide 10's 'The tie-break is risk, not fit' is asserted rather than evidenced by any risk criterion in the slide 7 screen — risk is not one of the three criteria, so the tie-break comes from outside the stated method. That is a logic break a client will find.

Craft: neither is distinctive. A's dark title slide and coloured pills give it slightly more personality, but the personality is inconsistent. B is plainer and more template-like in its component vocabulary, yet it is the one I would send unchanged — the argument holds, every chart carries a takeaway and a source, and nothing needs to be re-explained in the room.

Both are generic: A and B could both be re-skinned for any three-option screen with new labels. B is arguably the more generic-looking of the two (blue/orange/green default palette, plain sans, boxy cards) but its structure is purpose-built for this brief in a way A's is not.

Both decks clear integrity and legibility: no clipping, placeholders or empty frames I can see in either, and reading order is unambiguous on every page of both. So the decision falls to levels 3–5.

Coherence (3): both are internally consistent. B repeats one system rigorously — kicker label, one-line assertive title, then either a hero number, a five-column criteria strip (pages 5, 6, 7) or a full comparison table (page 8) — and the option pages 5/6/7 are literally interchangeable in structure, which is exactly what a three-option comparison needs. A is also consistent (green rule, footer, page numbers), but its callout boxes are unevenly filled: the EUR 14m box on page 2 and the 'c. EUR 5m / yr' box on page 6 have large trapped white space under the number, and page 12 leaves the bottom half of the slide empty below 'Thank you — questions and discussion'.

Communicative effectiveness (4): near parity, both title pages with conclusions ('Wider centralisation buys more savings, at a cost' vs 'Full centralisation saves the most on paper; Option 3 captures the value at far lower risk'), both caption their chart. A's page 8 chart is the weaker artefact: it plots +14 (duplicated cost) against -9 and -5 (savings) on one axis, so the sign convention has to be rescued by a footnote; B's page 9 chart keeps a single savings scale with the cost case below zero and reads without explanation. A does one thing better — the green-tinted Option 3 row on the page 9 risk table makes the recommendation visible before the text says it; B's page 10 risk table leaves 'Not applicable' sitting in a mitigation cell, which reads like a gap.

Craft and distinctiveness (5): this is the gap. B's page 3 centralisation spectrum, the three stat cards on page 2, the hero-number-plus-rationale option pages and the generous margins read as a composition built for this decision. A reads as a standard consulting shell — green header rule, 'Prepared for the Executive Committee', bulleted body with a grey number box on the right — that would look identical for a pricing review or a systems migration; its body copy is also noticeably smaller and denser (pages 4–7) for a committee-room deck.

B is the one I would send unchanged; A would need the empty box space and the mixed-sign chart fixed first.

Both decks clear integrity — no clipping, no placeholders, twelve slides each with consistent footers and numbering. The separation starts at legibility. A pushes several pages to a type size that stops working at the back of a room: slide 12 crams three columns (Risk / Mitigation / Decisions needed today) of multi-line body text plus a 'Next' footnote into one page; slide 10 stacks five long bullets over an eleven-item role list with no breathing room; slide 11's two quarter columns each carry five dense bullets. B never asks the reader to work that hard — its densest pages (slide 8's three-column change table, slide 9's role-by-role table) stay at a readable size with fewer rows. At visual coherence both are disciplined, but A mixes blue, orange and green accents with a colour logic that only sometimes tracks the three segments (slides 3 and 6 use it meaningfully; slide 11's orange/blue quarter headers and slide 1's orange-and-grey dashed bar do not), while B's eyebrow / title / footer system repeats identically on all twelve pages. On communicative effectiveness A has one genuine advantage: the before/after org charts on slides 5 and 6 show the structure a reader of an org-design proposal actually wants, and B's equivalent — slide 6, 'Shared delivery gives every segment the same bench' — is only four bullets and a black 'Shared Delivery Pool' bar, which is the weakest page in the deck. B also leaves slide 7 underloaded (140 / 11 / 7 floating in white space) and its slide 4 bar chart has an ambiguous y-axis label. But B's titles are consistently conclusions ('Geography made sense once. It doesn't anymore.', 'Customers buy by segment. We're organised by geography.', 'Seven of you are directly affected'), every number carries a unit line, and the density on each page matches what the page is for — whereas A's slides 10 and 12 are over-dense in a way that defeats the purpose in a live leadership session. On craft and distinctiveness it is not close: A reads as a standard corporate template with the blanks filled in — blue title bars, orange callouts, generic stat cards on slide 4 — and would look identical for any other brief. B reads as a document composed for this one: the editorial serif, the 62% panel on slide 3, the segment bench treatment, the closing 'Questions and discussion' in italic on slide 12. B wins clearly; A's org charts are the one thing worth stealing.

Integrity: both render cleanly with no clipping or placeholders, so the decision moves up the rubric. Legibility: A's charts are readable — bar labels, value callouts (e.g. 61.4 vs 63.0 on slide 4, 18.2 vs 17.5 on slide 5) and legends sit at usable size. B's charts on slides 3-7 are near-illegible: the four panels on slide 3 have tiny axis text and unlabelled black/grey bars, and the single-series bars on 4-7 carry no data labels at all, so the reader must infer the numbers from the title. B's slide 3 also renders bars in near-black and mid-grey with no encoded meaning, and the deltas are absent. Visual coherence: A repeats a consistent pattern — eyebrow, conclusion title, chart left, 'Why we missed / Why we beat plan / Why coverage fell short' reasons right, and a colour-coded variance chip top-right (-2.5%, +0.7pt, -20%, -13) that reads as a system. B has a consistent footer and page numbering (a real plus) but its variance slides are just title + bare bar + bullet block, and its slide 2 executive summary is a plain five-bullet list. Communicative effectiveness: A's titles state the conclusion and carry the number ('Revenue: EUR 61.4m, EUR 1.6m below the EUR 63.0m plan'), the initiative portfolio on slide 8 is a labelled donut with per-initiative status, slide 9 breaks the three off-plan initiatives into status-chipped cards, slide 11 gives each decision an 'THE ASK / WHY IT MATTERS / decision needed from' structure, and slide 12 recaps all four KPIs as chips with deltas. B's slide 9 lumps five initiatives into two undifferentiated boxes, and its slide 11 decisions are unstructured paragraphs in grey boxes. Craft: B's slide 1 black cover with the ash-grey chart palette is arguably more distinctive as a mark, and its footer discipline is better than A's (A has no page numbers or footer at all, and A's slide 2 has an awkward floating 'Asking today' line stranded near the bottom of an otherwise empty middle). But those are level-5 refinements that cannot offset B's level-2 chart legibility failures and level-4 missing data labels. Both are somewhat generic — A leans on stock Google-blue accents, B on a monochrome-plus-status-chip system — but A is the one I would send.

A wins clearly.

Both decks are structurally sound at the integrity level — no clipping, no placeholder text, no overlaps visible in either. A's slide 4 loop diagram, slide 6 three-lever cards and slide 10 milestone chevrons all sit inside their frames; B's slide 4 chain diagram and slide 11 timeline likewise. So the decision falls to levels 2–5.

Legibility: A is stronger. B leans on very small body type — the slide 4 chain boxes ('Turnover 44% / Institutional knowledge leaves with every agent'), the slide 7 table cells and the slide 12 measures table are set at a size that will not read from a board table, and B's slide 3 chart axis labels and the right-hand annotation block are near-marginal. A's metric cards (slide 3 '12 / 54% / +38% / 44%') and its target blocks on slides 7–9 are set large and are readable at distance. B's use of near-black-on-white throughout is safe but flat; A's colour coding (red for the problem, green for the plan) carries meaning without breaking contrast.

Coherence: A repeats a genuine system — coloured left rule + eyebrow + statement title on every slide, and a consistent right-hand 'PRIMARY TARGET' card with value / 6-month / 12-month on slides 7, 8 and 9. That repetition is the deck's spine. B is coherent but looser: the metric cards on slide 2 are a stacked right column, slide 5 and 6 use a different stat-block treatment, slide 7 uses a bare table, and slide 12 another table — the repeated elements do not repeat as tightly.

Communicative effectiveness: A wins clearly here. Its titles conclude ('NPS fell because three operating metrics moved together', 'Two fixes, one lever each — the system pulled both back', 'Twelve months, four checkpoints, in sequence'), and its slide 5 does the single most important job in this brief — it names each of the two prior failed attempts and, in a fixed What we did / What happened / What it missed structure, explains why each failed. B's equivalent (slide 7) reduces the same content to a three-column table with two rows of one-line text and a small closing sentence; it is thinner on the point the board most needs answered. A's slide 4 also makes the causal loop explicit ('which feeds back into turnover — the cycle compounds') and lands it on the customer-felt outcome 'NPS 41 → 12'; B's slide 4 chain is a flat left-to-right sequence with no closure of the loop, so the deck's central claim that the three metrics are one system is asserted rather than shown. A's slide 11 also adds a governance block explaining how the measures stay honest — a direct answer to a board that has been disappointed twice. A does have gaps: the slide 3 metric cards and slide 7–9 target blocks carry no source line, whereas B sources its chart on slide 3 and its diagram on slide 4.

Craft and distinctiveness: A's slide 6 numbered lever cards with 'PRIMARY MOVERS' tags, slide 10's four-checkpoint chevrons and slide 12's numbered approval asks with a closing pull-quote read as composed for this brief. B is competent monochrome that would look identical for a strategy deck on any topic — its slide 8 three-column plan and slide 11 milestone rail are the most template-like pages in either deck.

B's advantages are real but narrower: a genuine plotted trend line on slide 3 (A only states the numbers), consistent sourcing, and a calmer, more restrained aesthetic. That does not offset A's stronger typographic hierarchy, tighter repeated system, sharper conclusion-bearing titles and materially better treatment of the failed-attempts and loop arguments. A is the deck I would send.

Integrity: both render cleanly with no clipping, empty frames or placeholder text; A's densest pages (slide 8's five-column intervention table, slide 12's chart-plus-three-column recap) stay inside their boxes, and B's divider slides and tables are equally intact. No decision at level 1.

Neither is send-ready without a pass, but only A has defects a client would see on first flip.

Both clear Level 1 and 2: nothing is clipped, no placeholders survive, body copy and table type are readable in both, and reading order is linear in both. The separation happens at Level 3. B holds one visual system across all seven pages — every table (p3 headcount bridge, p4 levers and hiring plan, p6 cost comparison) uses the same black header band with white caps and the same alternating body rows, headings are the same Title Case sans at the same scale, and the four p1 callouts (+160 / 26% / 62% / £670k) are formatted identically with a caption of equal weight under each. A's tables drift: the p3 bridge has a heavy grey header, the p5 run-rate and investment tables are rule-only with no header fill, and the p6 investment table is a third, near-borderless treatment; its p1 KPI row also breaks its own repeat, with '67% ▲ +160 heads' carrying two figures and a two-line caption while the other three are single figures, and the first caption reads 'Not headcount growth needed', which looks like a typo for 'Net'. B's blemishes are rhythm-level, not system-level: p5 has a large void between the campus-hiring paragraph and 'The Retention Plan', and 'What This Costs Against the Current Run Rate' opens three lines from the foot of p5 before its table lands on p6. At Level 4, A is genuinely ahead — the To/From/Date/Re block addressed to the Managing Partners, the bridge table that includes a 'Today (Sep 2026)' opening row and a Net change column, the run-rate table stating blended fully-loaded cost per FTE ($150,000 → $142,000) and the change row, investment expressed as % of today's run rate, an explicit Key assumptions list, and four numbered decisions. B answers the same questions (bridge with 3-Year Total, £2.75M vs £4.76M cost comparison, per-level hiring plan) but without the assumptions or the decision list, and both documents lack any chart or cited source. Because a Level 3 failure outranks a Level 4 advantage, B wins — but only slightly, and A's memo framing and assumption disclosure would be the better paper if its table styling were unified. On genericness: A reads the more generic of the two, a default Word memo whose section furniture would suit any planning brief; B is also close to a stock consulting layout, but the statistic band and the consistent dark table language give it a small amount of specific identity. Neither is something I would send unchanged with my name on it.

Integrity: both are complete and neither clips, and both repeat the same flaw of a bare 'Contents' heading on page 1 with no table of contents under it (A p1 bottom-left, B p1 mid-page), so that cancels out. Both also let a findings table break across a page with the header row not repeated (A p7 opens mid-row with 'structure skips from H1 directly to H3'; B p6 opens with the orphaned fragment 'is not programmatically indicated'). Legibility is where they separate: A's findings tables (pp4-12) allocate column widths badly — 'Location', 'Impact' and 'Shared component' are squeezed to one or two words per line, producing cells 15+ lines tall with 'Payment — add/edit card' and 'Screen-reader users cannot determine what button they are on' broken into vertical ribbons; the ID column is wide enough to be wasted while the prose columns are starved. B's equivalent tables (pp5-8) give the 'Location & issue' and 'Remediation' columns real width and keep WCAG SC/Effort narrow, so lines run at a readable measure. Coherence: B carries a running header ('Customer Portal · WCAG 2.1 AA Accessibility Audit') and a 'Confidential — Internal Distribution Only' footer on every page, plus consistent dark table header bands; A has no running furniture at all and its tables alternate between having and lacking header bands. Communicative: B adds a severity summary with % of total (p4), a shared-design-system component table naming Form Field / Date Picker / Primary Button with blocker instances (p4), a person-day effort key with S/M/L definitions and a roll-up with suggested timelines (p9), and a retest schedule with owners and targets (p11); A gives effort as bare S/M/L letters with no key and a thinner retest table. Distinctiveness: A reads as default Word with an ad-hoc four-number band on p1; B has a deliberate cover (kicker, metadata block, classification line) and a 31/6/14/11 stat row on p2, though the amber tint on only the Serious and Moderate rows of the p4 summary is unexplained. Neither is fully client-ready without fixing the empty Contents, but B is the one I'd send after that fix.

A fails at level 1 on an element the brief explicitly required: page 1 carries a 'Table of Contents' heading with nothing beneath it — the heading is immediately followed by '1. Executive Summary'. An empty TOC reads as an unfilled placeholder, and it is unrecoverable because A has no page numbers anywhere (no footer or folio on any of its seven pages), so a TOC could not function even if populated. B's page 2 delivers a real Contents list with entries down to third-level items (2.1 Traffic and performance, 3.3 Side-by-side comparison) and dot leaders. Below that, A also breaks the comparison table across pages 3→4, leaving a single orphan row ('Control & customization') stranded at the top of page 4 above the section-4 continuation text. On coherence, A's table treatments disagree page to page — the 2.1 baseline-metrics table on page 2 is a plain two-column rule-only block, while the page-3 cost table is a full grid with a shaded header — and there is no running header, footer or accent system tying pages together; several pages (5, 7) start with a bare numbered list before their heading appears further down. B repeats a running header ('API Gateway Migration — Technical Report') and footer ('Platform Engineering · Internal') on every page, uses one dark-header table style consistently (3.3 comparison, 2.3 custom plugins, page-5 continuation with the header row correctly repeated), and opens with a composed cover: red 'PLATFORM ENGINEERING · TECHNICAL REPORT' eyebrow, two-line title, subtitle stating the comparison axes, rule, and prepared-by/date/version line. B is also more informative: page 4–5 enumerates all eleven plugins with function and native-equivalent status rather than asserting the 9/11 figure in prose, and its metric callouts (4,200 req/s, 180ms, 1.5 days/mo) carry unit labels underneath. B's real weakness is density, not integrity: page 3 (Executive Summary) is roughly two-thirds empty, page 5 ends after five table rows, and page 9's open questions fill less than a third of the page — the one-section-per-page rule wastes a lot of paper. A's page 1 callout block is arguably the single nicest element across both documents. But a level-1 failure plus missing pagination outranks B's level-4 whitespace problem.

A fails the integrity bar outright: page 6 renders completely blank, and page 8 carries only a stranded two-line paragraph ("Recommended cadence: review all six metrics weekly...") floating at the top with the rest of the page empty — the tail of the 'What to Measure' section has broken off its parent page. B has no empty or orphaned pages; all five pages carry the content the author intended. That lower-level failure outranks everything above it. Beyond integrity, A's page 2 and 3 KPI stacks ('47 min', '10 min', '37 min' vertically; '31%' and '6%' on page 3) leave more than half the page blank and read as vertical lists rather than a metric band, and A's page 7 metrics table is squeezed into four narrow columns that wrap almost every cell ('Wall-clock pipeline duration (p50 / p95)' breaking over four lines). B's page 1 puts the same three figures in a single horizontal KPI band with labels underneath, and its four tables (Measurements with a Total row, Recommendations with savings/priority/notes, the afterwards metrics table with target and 'Why it matters') are dimensioned to their content and repeat the same header rule and row rhythm across pages 2-5. B is not flawless — the third KPI on page 1 splits '4.7x  +37' from its 'min' unit onto a second line, the 'Priority' header on page 4 breaks as 'Prio rity', and pages 3-5 end high on the page leaving large lower voids — but these are cosmetic, not structural. Both documents are fairly generic in visual language (plain serif-free headings, hairline tables, one accent-free palette); neither would look specific to this brief if the numbers were swapped, though B's KPI band and the savings/priority columns at least shape the page around the audit's argument. B is sendable after fixing the unit wrap; A is not sendable with a blank page in it.

A has integrity and legibility failures that outrank its strengths. Page 3 of A opens with an orphaned bullet list ('Forecast demand growth of 38% assumes...') that has no heading — the section 2.1 Methodology text on page 2 runs across the break into a bare list, and the page starts mid-thought. Page 5 of A is worse: it begins with the fragment 'engineering estimate that needs validation against the pipeline's actual storage-vs-age profile' and its running body text is set at a markedly smaller size than pages 1–4, so type size is inconsistent within one document — a legibility and coherence failure on the same page. A's tables are also badly proportioned: the 3.4 Lever Comparison table on page 5 has five cramped columns where 'Key risk' and 'Time to effect' wrap to four and five lines each ('Fast (vendor-dependent, ~weeks)'), and the 2.2 Quarterly Projection table on page 3 wraps every status cell. The 2.3 breach table on page 3 and the continuation table on page 4 are the same table split across a page break with the header repeated but no continuation label, and the top of page 4 leads with a headerless table. B clears integrity: no clipping, no orphaned fragments, every page has a running header ('Capacity Forecast · Infrastructure Engineering'), a footer ('Confidential — Internal Distribution'), and page numbers, so repeated elements actually repeat — which A has none of. B's KPI strip on page 1 (47% / 38% / 71% / 7) carries full unit captions under each figure; A's identical strip uses a tiny caption that is harder to read at the same distance. On communicative effectiveness B is ahead: its tables carry source lines ('Source: internal capacity model, trailing 12-month storage consumption') and units in the column heads (vCPU-hrs/month, TB), and the levers table on page 3 gives Effect and Primary risk with quantified figures inline ('$5,890/month, or $69K annualised'). A's numbers are frequently unitless index values ('Compute index (Q0=100) 108') with no absolute quantity anywhere. B's decision section names an owner and a needed-by date (December 15, 2026). Neither is distinctive — both are conventional single-column report layouts with black-and-white tables and no chart at all, which for a capacity forecast with a month-seven breach is a real miss on both sides; B's dark-header tables are its only visual signature. B wins clearly because A fails at levels 1 and 2 where B does not.

A fails Integrity and Legibility before any higher criterion can help it. Page 2 of A contains a 'Table of Contents' heading followed by a single literal line reading 'Table of Contents' — an unrendered/placeholder TOC field, an outright empty page. The retention table on A's pages 6–7 breaks across a page boundary and the continuation on page 7 repeats the header row then collapses into a fragment ('Retention) documents.') sitting above unrelated body text; the same table's Description/Retention columns are so narrow that entries wrap to five or six lines of tiny type ('Access, security, and application error logs across production systems'). A's page 10 opens mid-sentence with an orphaned 'Mitigation' paragraph detached from its 4.2 parent, and A's page 16 ends with sections 8.1/8.2 while section 7's subsections (7.3–7.5) sit on pages 14–15 with no visual anchor. Body type across A is uniformly small and grey with no size differentiation between section body and table cells, and the section numbering (4.1/4.2/4.3, 7.1–7.5) restarts hierarchy visually without indentation cues.

B clears Integrity: no empty page, no placeholder, no broken table. Its retention table on page 3 fits on one page with a dark header band, readable column widths, an explicit 'Conflict?' column and a footnote explaining how periods run from the trigger event — this is the single most load-bearing artifact in the brief and B renders it whole while A splinters it. Legibility holds: consistent margins, a running header ('Data Retention Policy'), a footer ('Confidential — Internal Use Only'), and a hierarchy where H1 section titles are visibly larger than body text. Coherence holds across all seven pages: the same header/footer, the same heading scale, consistent left-aligned block paragraphs.

On communicative effectiveness B is also stronger on the brief's hard requirement: the three conflicts are resolved in 6.1–6.3 with a repeated four-part structure (Privacy position / Tax position / Resolution / Justification) that mirrors the table's Conflict column, and section 4 names the current manual state before proposing 'Automated Lifecycle Management' with a 'Manual Deletion Fallback' — a directly actionable answer. A does attempt the same structure (4.1–4.3) but buries it after a broken table and splits one instance across a page break.

Both are generic in look — B is a competent Word-default policy document with one styled table and no distinctive typographic voice; A is barely styled at all. Neither reaches level 5. But B is sendable unchanged; A is not, on the placeholder TOC and broken table alone.

Both clear integrity: no clipping, no placeholder text, tables complete in both. Level 2 is a wash — A sets larger body type, B is denser but still comfortable for a print report. The separation starts at level 3. A's page 1 stops around 60% of the page after the 'Impact' paragraph and leaves the bottom two-fifths empty before the Timeline breaks to page 2, and its Remediation table splits so page 4 opens with a repeated header plus a single orphan row ('Gate failover completion on confirmed load-balancer convergence') before the next H2 — the vertical rhythm is inconsistent page to page. B carries a running header ('Post-Incident Report — ICS-1') and a 'Confidential — Internal Distribution Only' footer on all three pages, and its columns fill consistently; repeated elements actually repeat. Level 4 is where B pulls decisively ahead: its KPI band carries four figures (1,842 orders / 214 duplicated, annotated 11.6% / 19 min to detect / 4h 00m total) against A's three (A omits the 19-minute detection figure the brief called out, and gives no denominator context for 214); B's timeline adds an 'Elapsed' column so the 11-minute dual-write window and 96-minute diagnosis are readable as durations rather than inferred from clock times; and B's Remediation table has 'Target Date' with concrete dates (2026-09-19, 2026-10-03) and named owners (M. Chen, A. Okafor, D. Fontaine, R. Singh), where A gives vague 'Target' spans ('2 weeks', '3 weeks') plus a 'Status' column reading mostly 'Not started', which communicates less. B's causes are numbered and each states the mechanism plus consequence; A's cause 3 ('Runbook was eleven months out of date') runs as loose prose. Level 5: neither is distinctive — both are stock report typography — but A's oversized numeral band is the only real design gesture, and it is undercut by the half-empty page 1. B is the one I would send.

Integrity: both render without clipping, but A's page 1 has a visible defect — the first line of body text on page 2 ('run and a run with the payments service connection pool enlarged from 200 to 500 concurrent connections') is an orphaned continuation floating above the 'Test Runs and Results' heading with no header/rule to anchor it, and the same happens on page 3 ('Run 2 falling fast...'). A's page 2 table is also cramped: the 'Checkout p99 at Limiting Resource' column header runs together and the Run 2 cell wraps to five ragged lines inside a narrow column. B's tables on pages 2 and 3 sit in clean, evenly weighted columns with dark header bands and no wrap collisions. Legibility: A's page 1 stat block ('3.2x / 2.4x / 3.1x') has captions set so small they are nearly unreadable at print size; B's equivalent row carries the same three figures at a legible caption size and adds a '+0.7x' delta marker. Visual coherence: B repeats a running header ('Checkout Platform — Load Testing') and a footer ('Confidential — Internal Distribution Only') on every one of its five pages, and its tables share one consistent header treatment; A has no header or footer at all, so pages 2–4 read as loose sheets, and A's only table (page 2) has a different, lighter styling than anything else in the document. Communicative effectiveness: B structures the runs as two labelled sub-sections ('Run 1 — Baseline Infrastructure (Payments Pool = 200)', 'Run 2 — Remediated Infrastructure (Payments Pool = 500)') each with its own multiplier-by-p99 table including a Result column that names the exact failure ('FAIL — pool exhausted', 'FAIL — write-lock contention'), and adds a fixes table on page 4 with Status / Expected Ceiling / Effect columns; A presents a single flat run table and delivers the fixes as prose bullets with no expected-ceiling column. B also states units consistently (ms, concurrent connections, utilisation percentages) and gives a subtitle and prepared-by line on page 1. Craft: B's cover block with title, subtitle, byline and stat row is composed; A's page 1 is a title over unstyled paragraphs. Both are somewhat generic corporate report shells, but A is the more template-like of the two because it has no repeating furniture to make it feel authored. A's advantage — nothing — does not offset failures at levels 1 and 3. Both end with a weak final page (A p4, B p5) where a short paragraph and a numbered list sit alone in the top third, leaving two-thirds blank; that is a shared flaw and does not separate them.

Both clear level 1-2: neither page shows clipped, overflowing, or placeholder content; the four-column comparison table fits the measure in both, type sizes are comfortable, and reading order is unambiguous on all four pages. The separation happens at levels 3-5.

Visual coherence: B repeats a running header ('Event Pipeline — Broker Selection') and a footer ('Memo — Engineering') on both pages, so page 2 is visibly the same document as page 1. A has no header or footer at all, so its page 2 opens cold on a mid-sentence continuation ('already understood operationally but is provisioned for 30,000 messages per second...') with nothing identifying the document — the two sheets do not read as a set. B's addressing block (To / From / Date / Re on stacked bold-labelled lines) is a repeated, structured element; A compresses the same four fields into one small italic run under the title, which is tidier but weaker as hierarchy.

Communicative effectiveness: B puts 'Recommendation' first on page 1 — 'We recommend Option C, the managed broker, at EUR 5,100 per month' — before Requirements and the table, which is the correct shape for a decision memo; the reader gets the answer in the first two lines. A defers the recommendation to the bottom of page 1, after Requirements and the options table, so the conclusion arrives last. B's table cells are decision-grade and scannable ('Caps at 30k', 'Sunk, already running', 'EUR 5,100'), and the small note under it discloses that ordering, replay and operational fit for B and C are stated at parity with the brief — an explicit evidence caveat attached to the table it qualifies. A carries the same honesty inside the cells ('Assumed met — verify under target load'), which is good, but it bloats the cells and pushes the table wider than it needs to be. B also names its counter-case explicitly with a 'Why Not A or B' heading; A folds the same reasoning into an unlabelled recommendation paragraph.

Craft: B's page 2 heading 'What Would Change This Recommendation' with four conditional bullets each stating a numeric trigger (36k msg/s, 50,000 msg/s at volume, EUR 5,100/month against a hard budget) is more disciplined than A's equivalent bullets, which restate the option trade-offs rather than the trigger.

Both end with roughly half of page 2 blank, and both are recognisably Word-memo generic — the same shell would serve any recommendation memo. B is slightly less so because of the header/footer system, the shaded table header and the table caption. B wins clearly, not decisively: A has no defect below level 3, it simply organises the argument less well and abandons its second page visually.

Both are clean, single-column, red-rule-accented Word standards with no clipping, no placeholder text, and consistent running heads/footers, so both clear Integrity and Legibility. They separate at levels 3–5. A (second image) fails nothing but is denser and more complete: it has a Document Control block (Standard ID, version, supersedes, next review) on p1, a contents list that carries the same section numbering used downstream, and its tables carry the implementation detail an engineer needs — p4 field table with a Required column that distinguishes Always vs Conditional and gives concrete examples (RFC 3339 with millisecond precision, http.method/route/status_code conditions), p5 metric table with Type/Unit/Required labels (histogram bucket boundaries specified in seconds on p4/p5), p6 retention table split into Hot/queryable, Archive and Deletion columns plus a legal-hold note, and p8 a per-quarter milestone table with explicit exit criteria. B (first image) covers the same sections but thinner: its p5 retention table is three rows with vaguer notes, its p3 RED metrics section is two short lines, and p8 (Exemption Process) and p10 (Appendix A) are one-third-full pages with an enormous white void below, which reads as an under-filled template page rather than an intentional composition. B's p6 also leaves roughly 60% of the page empty under three KPI numerals. B does have one nice touch A lacks — the 12/34, 21/34, 4 stat row on p6 giving the gap assessment an immediate read — but A answers the same brief line with a four-column gap table (gap, current state, required state, deadline) that is more implementable, which is what the brief asked for. On communicative effectiveness A's headings and tables state conclusions and conditions; B's leave more to interpretation. Both are template-flavoured (Word default look, red hairline rules, pink-tinted table headers) and neither is distinctive, so level 5 is a wash. A wins on completeness and page-level density discipline; B loses points for three visibly starved pages.

Both share the same Level-1 defect — page 1 carries a 'Contents' heading with nothing under it (A between the KPI band and '1. Overview and constraints'; B between the metadata line and 'Executive Summary'), so neither clears Integrity cleanly and the tie-break moves to how much else is wrong. A adds a second integrity/legibility problem the reader will hit: the failure-mode table breaks between pages 10 and 11 mid-row, so page 11 opens under a repeated 'Failure mode / Detection / Mitigation and response' header with the orphaned fragment 'does not parse cleanly' sitting in the Failure mode column, reading as a nonsense entry. On Legibility, A's body and table type is set noticeably smaller and lighter throughout — the page 10/11 failure-mode grid and the page 9 monitoring table wrap 'Dual-write partial failure (one column set succeeds, the other fails)' over five or six lines in a narrow column, and the page 2 constraint bullets are grey-on-white at a size that is hard work on paper. B sets the same material larger with more column width and reversed dark header rows on the Current/Target Schema, Migration Strategy, Monitoring and Failure Modes tables, so the reading order and the header/body distinction are obvious. On Visual coherence B is also ahead: a running header ('Orders Table Schema Migration Plan') and footer ('Confidential — Platform Engineering') repeat on all eight pages, and the red rule under every H1 repeats identically; A carries a status line only on page 1 and no running furniture at all, so pages 6 and 11 float with no identification. Communicatively both cover schema, four phases with exit criteria and rollback, backfill monitoring and failure modes; B edges it by adding a Phase column to the failure-modes table (page 7) and a self-contained Appendix rollback summary with data-loss risk and time-to-rollback (page 8), and by pairing units to its cover metrics ('6,000 writes /sec', '31 hours'), where A's cover labels are set so small they are near-illegible. A's one genuine advantage is the more editorial cover — serif italic subtitle over the big-number band — but it does not survive the smaller type and split table below it. On genericness both read as templates rather than as documents made for this brief: B is the more overtly corporate one (red accent rule, dark header rows, confidential footer — swap the title and it serves any engineering plan), while A is a plain numbered-report shell; neither uses a diagram, a phase timeline or any visual that would make a four-deploy dual-write window legible at a glance, which is the one thing this brief was asking to be shown rather than listed. I would send neither unchanged with my name on it — both need the empty Contents resolved first — but B needs materially less work.

A fails integrity on page 1: the cover is entirely blank (title, report date and assessment period only appear on pages 2-3, which are themselves near-empty half-filled pages), so three of seventeen pages carry a handful of lines each while the running text elsewhere sits in a dense single column with no header/footer at all — the 'Confidential — internal distribution only' classification floats alone at the top of page 3 with nothing anchoring it. B has no such gaps: every page from the cover onward is populated, and the 'Authentication Service — Security Review — Confidential' running header plus 'Confidential — Internal Distribution Only' footer repeat on all 11 pages, giving the document an obvious frame and page identity. On visual coherence, A's findings table (page 7) is a bare unstyled grid with a hairline rule and coloured severity words, and its detailed findings run as undifferentiated prose blocks; B's findings table (page 4) has a filled dark header row with proper ID/Finding/Severity/Status columns and consistent zebra-free banding, and every finding is introduced by a uniform 'Severity / Status / Affected component' metadata line before Reproduction and Remediation, so the repeated structure actually repeats. Both hit the same KPI treatment (9 / 2 / 4 / 3 findings) in the executive summary; A splits the nine-engineer-day figure into a caption below, B renders '9 eng-days' as a second sized statistic with an explanatory line, which reads more deliberate. Communicatively both cover scope, method, per-finding reproduction/remediation and residual risk, but B's contract is tighter — statuses are varied and specific (Open, Fixed with a date, Accepted risk, In remediation) and B's residual risk closes with an explicit 'Overall assessment ... Low-to-Medium' verdict, whereas A's residual-risk page trails into a numbered recommendation list that spills onto page 17 with only three lines on it. Both are generic in the same way — Helvetica-ish sans on white, one accent colour, no visual identity specific to a security engagement — but A's empty cover and orphan pages are a level-1 failure that outranks any advantage above it.
